# Harbor Customs Playbook

## Declare Stage

When I see my three crates, I calculate their sum immediately.

When deciding what to declare, I declare my true total value. This avoids the -40 penalty from being flagged and lets me score the full value of my hold minus duty.

When my heaviest crate is worth less than 40, I declare my true total without worry—the spot check won't flag me.

When I'm behind in standings late in the game, I don't increase my declaration beyond what's safe just to catch up. The marginal points from aggressive declaring don't compensate for the risk of the -40 flag penalty.

## Route Stage

When I declare my true value and my heaviest crate is clearly below my declaration, I take the main route. The main route gives me all three crates minus a 30% duty, which is better than losing my smallest crate to the night route's 15% duty.

I take the night route only when I have low-value crates and need to minimize the duty I pay, accepting the loss of my smallest crate as a trade-off. However, I should calculate the explicit tradeoff: night route saves 0.15 × declared value in duty but costs the value of my smallest crate. Only take night route if smallest crate value < 0.15 × declared value.

## General Strategy

I play conservatively and honestly. Declaring true value is safer than bluffing because the harbormaster's spot check is mechanical and will catch understated values.

I do not try to outguess other players' declarations. I focus on my own holds and route choices.

When I'm ahead, I maintain my lead with consistent, safe play. When I'm behind, I don't take unnecessary risks with inflated declarations—steady scoring across remaining rounds is more reliable than one aggressive round.

## What Worked This Episode

Honest declarations paired with the main route consistently delivered positive scores every round. I finished at +247, placing second overall behind Mirren. This confirms the core strategy: true declaration avoids the -40 flag penalty, and the main route maximizes crate retention when the heaviest crate is safely below my declaration.

The conservative approach held me competitive throughout and prevented catastrophic penalties. Even when trailing late in the game, the safe play protected my position.

## Edge Cases to Watch

I declared my true value in all six rounds and never experienced a flag. This suggests my true totals were consistently in safe ranges relative to my heaviest crate. If I ever draw a hold where my heaviest crate is unusually close to my total value, I should still declare true value—the penalty for flagging is too severe to justify understatement.

The night route calculation is specific: only choose night if (smallest crate value) < (0.15 × declared value). In this episode my holds had sufficient spread that this was never the case, so main route was always dominant.

# Harbor Customs Playbook

## Declaration Strategy

When I declare, I will calculate my true hold total and identify my heaviest crate. My declaration must be at least as high as my heaviest crate to avoid a -40 point flag penalty.

When my hold total is low to moderate (under 60 points), I will declare close to my true total, as the duty savings from underdecking are marginal and the risk of a flag is real.

When my hold total is moderate (60-75 points), I will declare my true total or very close to it. At this range, both main and night routes score similarly, so honesty is the safest baseline.

When my hold total is high (above 75 points), I have two options:
- Declare my true total if my heaviest crate is significantly below my true total, making a flag unlikely.
- Declare 5-10 points below my true total if my hold is unusually top-heavy (heaviest crate close to total), to reduce duty burden while staying safe.

I will always check the recent declaration history (last 2-3 rounds). If the table is consistently declaring in a narrow band, I should stay within or slightly above that range. Declaring far below table norms signals weakness and leaves points on the table.

In the final round, I will account for my current standing. If I am trailing, I may need to declare higher and accept more risk. If I am ahead, I can afford to be slightly more conservative but should not sacrifice significant point value unnecessarily.

## Route Strategy

Before choosing a route, I will calculate the net score for both options:
- **Main route score:** (hold value) - floor(0.30 × declared)
- **Night route score:** (hold value - smallest crate) - floor(0.15 × declared)

If main scores higher, I take main. If night scores higher, I take night. I will not default to main reflexively.

When my declared value is moderate (60-75), main and night usually tie or are very close. When they tie, I may take main because it has no confiscation risk, but I should still calculate rather than assume.

When my declared value is high (above 75), night route often wins because:
- The duty savings (0.15 vs 0.30) are substantial.
- The cost is only my smallest crate.
- If my smallest crate is worth less than the duty difference, night wins decisively.

I will do this calculation every round. I have fallen into the trap of "main is safer" too many times and left points on the table.

However, I discovered in Round 5 that when I declare conservatively (60 on a true hold of 60), I may not have my crate breakdown in front of me at the route stage. In such cases, I should either:
- Recall the actual crate values from memory, or
- If uncertain, default to main as the conservative choice since the hold is moderate.

## Position and Competition

I finished this episode in first place (273 points) ahead of Mirren (219), Krek (221), and Odalie (210). This validates the approach of declaring close to true value on moderate holds and calculating routes precisely.

Key observations:
- In Round 2, declaring 100 on a true hold of 103 and taking main route scored 85 points and won the round decisively.
- In Round 3, declaring 79 on a 79 true hold and taking main scored 62 points.
- In Round 4, declaring 56 on a 60 true hold and taking main was conservative but safe (scored 42).
- In Round 5, declaring 60 on a 60 true hold and taking main scored 42 points.
- In Round 6, declaring 55 on a 55 true hold and taking main scored 36 points.

I was conservative throughout but won the episode by being honest and calculating routes correctly. The other players' declarations ranged widely (23-101 across the five rounds I saw), suggesting that the table did not have a unified strategy.

The fact that I won despite never declaring more than 100 suggests that consistency and accuracy matter more than aggressive bluffing. However, I should not assume that this strategy will always work—in future episodes, if I have a genuinely high hold (above 85), I should declare it confidently rather than discount it.

Going forward: declare honestly near my true value, calculate routes precisely every round, and do not let excessive caution prevent me from capturing the full value of strong holds.

# Harbor Customs Playbook

**On Declaration:**

When I see my three crates, I will add their values and declare that total or very close to it. Honesty is my baseline; it keeps me safe from the spot check penalty that costs 40 points and recalculates duty at the higher rate.

I will always declare at least as much as my heaviest crate to avoid triggering the flag. This is non-negotiable.

When I'm unsure whether to declare exactly my true total or slightly higher, I'll declare my true total. The duty savings from understatement don't justify the downside risk.

**On Route Selection:**

When I have a moderate declaration that aligns with my true hand value, I will take the main route. The main route gives me floor(0.30 × declared value) duty and I keep all my crates.

I will consider the night route only if:
- My declared value is genuinely low and my smallest crate is small enough that losing it doesn't materially hurt my round score, AND
- The duty savings are material (the declared value is high enough that 0.15 vs 0.30 makes a real difference).

Even when night route saves duty, I should compare: (true total − smallest crate − duty at night) versus (true total − duty at main). Main route's simplicity and full retention of crates makes it the default safe play.

The six episodes show I took main route consistently through all rounds and achieved a final score of 258 points, finishing in a competitive position. Main route is my anchor.

**On Competitive Positioning:**

I will not let my current position in the standings distract me from sound individual-round decisions. Each round stands alone. Maximize this round's score; trust that consistency will handle the tournament.

In the final round, I do not need a special strategy. I apply the same honest declaration and safe route logic I use every other round.

**On Spotting When to Be Aggressive:**

If I ever find myself in a round where my declared value is significantly below my true total (more than 10–15 points below), I may be signaling weakness. In that case, night route becomes more coherent—the market interprets a low declaration as a weak hand anyway, so losing my smallest crate is less of a surprise.

However, the better play is to declare honestly and take main route. Don't engineer low declarations just to justify night route later. If I am declaring low, it should be because my hand truly is weak or because I've made an intentional strategic choice to understate—not by accident.

**On Sticking to the Playbook:**

My six-round record proves that honest declaration and consistent main-route play work. I never deviated from this strategy and finished strong. Do not second-guess this approach based on hypotheticals about what night route *might* save. The math and the results both favor my baseline: declare true value, take main route, keep all crates.

The temptation to optimize duty by taking night route is seductive but false. The reliability and simplicity of main route, combined with full crate retention, is the winning strategy over six rounds.

# Harbor Customs Playbook

## Declaration Strategy

When you see your three crates, sum their values immediately. Always declare at least the value of your heaviest crate—this is non-negotiable to avoid the -40 penalty flag.

Beyond the safety floor, declare your true total value. The math consistently favors honesty: the duty penalty is manageable when you keep all your crates on the main route, and lying risks catastrophic -40 swings that wreck your score.

When you're trailing in points with rounds remaining, resist the urge to declare far above your hand's value hoping to bluff. Look at what others have declared in recent rounds—your declarations should stay within the range established by the table. Declarations that deviate wildly upward invite suspicion and won't improve your final score if you get caught.

Playing honest declarations at your true value has proven itself twice now: you finished at +303 in the first recorded episode and +261 in this one, despite being behind in the leaderboard going into the final round both times. This validates the strategy completely.

However, I notice that when I was ahead on the final leaderboard (234 to Krek's 221 entering round 6), declaring my true value of 57 and choosing main still delivered a solid score (+261 final), so the strategy works whether leading or trailing. The consistency of this approach across different position states confirms it is sound.

## Route Selection

Always take the main route. I have succeeded by choosing main every single time across six rounds in both episodes. The night route's math looks tempting—lower duty at 0.15—but losing your smallest crate is a hidden tax that compounds over the game. The main route's higher duty (0.30 vs 0.15) is more than offset by keeping all three crates in hand.

Do not chase variance in any round. A safe, predictable main route score is worth more than gambling on night route luck, especially when the final leaderboard is tight.

## Positional Thinking

Track the leaderboard after each round, but do not let it drive you to reckless declarations. Your job is to maximize your own score per round, not to beat specific players.

Trailing going into round 6 in this episode (234 vs Mirren's 219), you stayed disciplined and honest rather than overbidding, and ended at +261. This confirms that steady, honest play on the main route closes gaps and maintains leads better than desperate declarations in endgame.

In the final round especially, whether you're ahead or behind: do not overreach. A solid, safe score on main route is better than a speculative high declaration that risks a flag and -40.
